qt: to the Commission Maria Zacharia (NI) Subject:

Life sciences graduates in Greece, particularly graduates in biology and related fields, have always faced serious inequality when it comes to the recognition of professional qualifications. They have significantly restricted or no access to professional activities that are available to graduates of equivalent faculties in other Member States. This issue appears to be linked to the continued existence of closed professions or fragmented laws governing professions with no clear proportionality assessment, in spite of the requirements of Directive (EU) 2018/958 on a proportionality test before adoption of new regulation of professions, and the principles of free movement of workers and freedom of establishment. This situation is creating real distortions in the labour market and could lead to the unequal treatment of graduates with equivalent qualifications within the Union. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Has it looked into whether the existing restrictions faced by life sciences graduates in Greece with regard to accessing regulated professions are compatible with Directive (EU) 2018/958 and the principles of proportionality and non-discrimination under EU law?
Does it consider that continued exclusion from regulated professions without a substantiated proportionality assessment may constitute an infringement of Articles 45 and 49 TFEU?
Does it intend to ask the Greek authorities for information/data on the comparative treatment of life sciences graduates in Greece and other Member States?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (12.10.2026) Directive (EU) 2018/9581 requires Member States to assess, before adoption, whether newly adopted or amended national rules restricting access to, or pursuit of, regulated professions are justified, proportionate and non-discriminatory. The Commission is not aware that Greece would have adopted new, or amended the existing legislation regarding life science professions following entry into force of the Directive, and in any event no such new rules have been notified via the Database of Regulated Professions; thus the procedural obligations under the Directive are not applicable. In any case, the Directive does not harmonise access requirements for regulated professions, which remain within the competence of Member States subject to the principles of nondiscrimination and proportionality2. Differences between Member States regarding access opportunities for life sciences graduates do not, in themselves, constitute a breach of EU law. The Commission monitors the Directive’s application in Greece, which has been transposed through Law 4763/20203. The Commission has not received relevant complaints from citizens or companies concerning the application of the Directive with regard to regulation of life sciences professions. Moreover, from the information provided to the Commission, there does not seem to be a cross-border element between Member States for the EU law to become applicable, as Articles 45 and 49 of the Treaty on the Functioning on the European Union do not generally apply to situations that are purely internal to a single Member State. Finally, the Commission is not aware of any problem regarding the recognition of life scientists qualifications in other Member States.

1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32018L0958. 2 Case C-575/11 Nasiopoulos v Ipourgos Igias kai Pronoias EU:C:2013:430, paras 19–20. 3 As amended by Part VI of Law 5291/2026 following Case C-518/24 European Commission v Hellenic
